objective: By the end of this lesson you can find and read the 14 CFR parts 1, 61 and 91 rules a flight instructor uses every week, apply 49 CFR part 830 to an accident or incident, explain what Advisory Circulars, SAFOs, InFOs, the ACS, the POH/AFM and the AIM are and how binding each one is, and teach a learner to answer "Is this legal?" from current sources.
why: Learners will ask you legal questions long after they stop asking about stalls, and they repeat your answers to their passengers. A CFI who knows which publication binds the pilot, and which one only helps the pilot comply, gives answers that hold up to an examiner, an inspector or the NTSB. Teaching a learner to look it up, instead of trusting memory, is the skill they keep.

prereading.what: The general definitions (look at night, operate, airplane) and the rules of construction for shall, may and includes.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 1.1 to 1.3

prereading.printed: 14 CFR parts 61 and 91, tables of contents
prereading.what: Read only the subpart and section titles. This is the map you will teach from.
prereading.label: 14 CFR parts 61 and 91 contents

prereading.what: All of part 830: definitions, immediate notification, preservation and reports.
prereading.label: 49 CFR 830.1 to 830.15

prereading.what: How the CFR is organized, the AIM, handbooks, Advisory Circulars and flight publications.
prereading.label: PHAK 1-7 to 1-12

prereading.what: AFM, POH and owner's manual, and the nine standard POH sections.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-1 to 9-5

prereading.what: What the AIM is, its publication schedule, its policy statement and how it treats ACs.
prereading.label: AIM front matter

prereading.what: Safety, accident and hazard reports: ASRS, accident reporting, near midair collisions, SAFOs and InFOs.
prereading.label: AIM 7-7-1 to 7-7-5

warmup: Think first: a learner tells you, "A guy in the FBO said the AIM says I can't take my sister flying at night unless I've done three night landings." Before you answer, which publication actually holds that rule, which paragraph, and which of the three "nights" in 14 CFR does it use?

key_terms.def: The codification of the general and permanent rules of federal agencies, in 50 titles; FAA rules are Title 14, Aeronautics and Space [[1:22|PHAK 1-7]].
14 CFR 1.3: how to read the words shall, may, no person may and includes [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
Making an outside document part of a regulation. Part 61 incorporates the ACS and PTS this way [[60:199|14 CFR 61.14]].
An occurrence between boarding with intent of flight and disembarking in which anyone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Hospitalization over 48 hours starting within 7 days, most bone fractures, severe bleeding or nerve, muscle or tendon damage, internal organ injury, or certain burns [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Damage that hurts structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement; part 830 lists exclusions [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
An occurrence other than an accident, associated with operating an aircraft, that affects or could affect safety [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
An FAA document of nonregulatory material; not binding unless a regulation incorporates it by reference [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].
Safety Alert for Operators: important, often time-critical safety information that may recommend non-regulatory action [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].
Information for Operators: like a SAFO but lower urgency, helping operators meet administrative or certain regulatory requirements [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].
A manufacturer document approved by the FAA, specific to a make and model and usually a serial number, with the airplane's procedures and limitations [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
A civil/military flight information publication issued every 56 days with airport, NAVAID, communication and special notice data [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]].

chunks.title: Binding or advice: a map of the publications

body.p: Every week a learner will ask, "Is that a rule or just a good idea?" Start any lesson on publications by sorting them into two piles: what binds the pilot, and what helps the pilot comply. The FAA sets safety standards through the Code of Federal Regulations, and its rules are Title 14 [[1:22|PHAK 1-7]].

head: Publication
Binding?
What it is for
rows: 14 CFR (parts 1, 61, 91 and others)
Yes, regulation
Definitions, pilot and instructor certification, and operating rules [[1:23|PHAK 1-8]].
49 CFR part 830 (NTSB)
Yes, regulation
Notifying and reporting accidents, incidents and overdue aircraft, and preserving wreckage and records [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]].
AFM or POH
Its operating limitations, markings and placards must be complied with [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]].
Procedures and limitations for that make and model, usually by serial number [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
ACS or PTS
The practical test consists of the tasks in the ACS/PTS that part 61 incorporates by reference [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]].
A testing standard, not a training syllabus [[24:30|AFH 1-9]].
AIM
No. It says it is not regulatory, but its techniques may be required by other regulations [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]].
Basic flight information and ATC procedures for the NAS [[33:52|AIM Basic Flight Information]].
Advisory Circulars
No, unless a regulation incorporates them by reference [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].
For example, an acceptable, clearly understood way to comply with a regulation [[1:25|PHAK 1-10]].
SAFOs and InFOs
No. A SAFO may recommend non-regulatory action [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].
Fast distribution of safety and operator information [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].

callout.text: Rule first, then help. The CFR says what you must do; the AC, AIM and POH often show how to do it. Teach learners to find the rule before they quote the help.

check.q: A learner says, "An AC said it, so it's mandatory." What does the AIM say about an AC's contents?
check.a: Unless incorporated into a regulation by reference, an AC's contents are not binding on the public [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].

chunks.title: K1: How 14 CFR is built and how to read a citation

body.p: The CFR has 50 titles. Title 14, Aeronautics and Space, covers civil aviation, and its Chapter I (Federal Aviation Administration) is divided into subchapters A through N [[1:22|PHAK 1-7]]. Show the learner the whole map before opening any one rule.

bullets: Part 1, definitions, sits in Subchapter A [[60:1|14 CFR Part 1]].
Part 43, maintenance, sits in Subchapter C, Aircraft [[60:127|14 CFR Part 43]].
Part 61, certification of pilots and instructors, sits in Subchapter D, Airmen [[60:174|14 CFR Part 61]].
Part 71, airspace designations, sits in Subchapter E, Airspace [[60:410|14 CFR Part 71]].
Part 91, general operating and flight rules, sits in Subchapter F [[60:418|14 CFR Part 91]].
Part 141, pilot schools, sits in Subchapter H [[60:767|14 CFR Part 141]].

body.p: Each part is split into subparts, then sections. Part 61 runs Subpart A General, B Aircraft Ratings, C Student Pilots, D Recreational, E Private, F Commercial, G Airline Transport, H Flight Instructors, I Ground Instructors and J Sport Pilots [[60:174|14 CFR Part 61 contents]] [[60:175|14 CFR Part 61 contents]] [[60:176|14 CFR Part 61 contents]] [[60:177|14 CFR Part 61 contents]]. Part 91 runs Subpart A General, B Flight Rules (general, VFR, IFR), C Equipment, Instrument and Certificate Requirements, D Special Flight Operations and E Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance and Alterations, with more after that [[60:419|14 CFR Part 91 contents]] [[60:421|14 CFR Part 91 contents]] [[60:422|14 CFR Part 91 contents]].

head: Piece of 14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)(i)
What it points to
rows: 14 CFR
Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations [[1:22|PHAK 1-7]]
Part 61, Certification: Pilots, Flight Instructors, and Ground Instructors [[60:174|14 CFR Part 61]]
Section 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]
Paragraph (b), night takeoff and landing experience [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]
The three takeoffs and landings to a full stop in the night period [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]
The person was sole manipulator of the controls [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]

callout.text: Teach the subpart titles before the sections. A learner who knows student pilot rules live in Subpart C of part 61 finds 61.87 in seconds instead of searching the whole part.

check.q: Which subchapter of Title 14, Chapter I holds part 91?
check.a: Subchapter F, Air Traffic and General Operating Rules [[60:418|14 CFR Part 91]].

chunks.title: K1: Part 1 definitions and the rules of construction

body.p: Part 1 has three sections: 1.1 general definitions, 1.2 abbreviations and symbols, and 1.3 rules of construction [[60:1|14 CFR 1.1]]. The 1.1 definitions apply throughout the chapter unless the context requires otherwise [[60:1|14 CFR 1.1]]. For example, an airplane is an engine-driven fixed-wing aircraft heavier than air, supported in flight by the dynamic reaction of the air against its wings [[60:1|14 CFR 1.1]].

bullets: Shall is used in an imperative sense [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
May is permissive: it states authority or permission [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
No person may, or a person may not, means no person is required, authorized or permitted to do the act [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
Includes means includes but is not limited to [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
Singular words include the plural, plural words include the singular, and masculine words include the feminine [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].

body.p: Each part can add its own definitions. 61.1(b) defines aeronautical experience, authorized instructor (a CFI in compliance with 61.197), complex airplane and cross-country time for part 61 [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1(b)]]. Teach learners to check both 1.1 and the part's own definitions section.

head: Rule
Period
What it controls
rows: 14 CFR 1.1, night
End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight, from the Air Almanac, converted to local time [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]
The general meaning of night throughout 14 CFR unless a rule sets its own period [[60:1|14 CFR 1.1]]
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]
To carry passengers in that period: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in that period within the preceding 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]
Sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]]
Lighted position lights to operate an aircraft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]]

callout.text: Teaching only one "night" is a classic instructor error. Give all three periods, with the rule for each, and have the learner write them on the same page of their notes.

check.q: Name the three "night" periods a learner meets in 14 CFR and the rule behind each.
check.a: Civil twilight to civil twilight (1.1) [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]; 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise for passenger currency (61.57(b)) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]; sunset to sunrise for position lights (91.209) [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

chunks.title: K1: Part 61 and part 91 sections to know cold

body.p: Part 61 covers certification of pilots, flight instructors and ground instructors: eligibility, knowledge, proficiency, training and testing. Part 91 covers general flight rules, VFR and IFR, and part 43 covers maintenance [[1:23|PHAK 1-8]]. These are the sections learners ask about most; know where each one is without looking.

head: Section
What it says, in short
The learner's question
rows: To serve as a required pilot, have your pilot certificate and a photo ID in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]].
"Do I need my certificate on me?"
To carry passengers: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings within the preceding 90 days as sole manipulator, same category, class and type; full stop in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].
"Can I take my friend up?"

A private pilot may not act as PIC for compensation or hire except as listed in (b) to (h), and may not pay less than the pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].
"Can my friends pay?"
The PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority on, the operation; in an emergency the PIC may deviate as needed and must send a written report if asked [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].
"Who decides?"
No operation unless airworthy; the PIC decides if the aircraft is in condition for safe flight and must stop the flight when unairworthy conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
"Is it safe to go?"
Comply with AFM limitations, markings and placards; a current, approved AFM must be available in the aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]].
"Do we need the POH aboard?"
No acting as a crewmember within 8 hours of drinking, while under the influence, or at 0.04 or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].
"Can I fly the morning after a party?"

Before each flight the PIC becomes familiar with all available information; runway lengths and takeoff and landing data for every flight, plus weather, fuel, alternatives and known delays for IFR or flights away from the airport [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].
"What do I have to check?"

A current airworthiness certificate and an effective registration certificate must be in the aircraft; the airworthiness certificate must be displayed [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]].
"What papers must be in the plane?"

Annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months; a 100-hour inspection if carrying persons for hire or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides; up to 10 hours over to reach the inspection place [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]] [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
"Does my airplane need a 100-hour?"

body.p: Other part 61 sections belong to other lessons: endorsements, the flight review (61.56), your 61.189 records and 61.197 recent experience are in AI.II.K, and your duties as an instructor are in FI.I.E.

check.q: Which two certificates must be in the aircraft under 91.203(a)?
check.a: An appropriate and current airworthiness certificate and an effective U.S. registration certificate [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]].

chunks.title: K1 in practice: answering "Is this legal?"

body.p: The AIH gives three steps for any learner question: be sure you understand it, answer as directly and accurately as you can, then check that the learner is satisfied. If you cannot answer, say so freely and promise to get the answer, or help the learner look it up [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. For a legal question, looking it up together is the lesson.

bullets: Restate the question: who is acting (PIC, student, instructor, operator), with what certificate, doing what, and when. (Application.)
Pick the part: people, certificates and currency are mostly part 61; operating the aircraft is part 91; accidents and incidents are 49 CFR 830 [[1:23|PHAK 1-8]] [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]].

Read the applicability section and definitions first: part 91 applies to operations within the United States, including waters within 3 NM of the coast [[60:435|14 CFR 91.1]]; part 61 adds its own definitions [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1(b)]].

Read the whole section, not the first line. 61.113(a) starts "Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h)" [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]], and 61.57(a)(1) starts "Except as provided in paragraph (e)" [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].
Apply 1.3: shall is a command, may is permission, includes is not a complete list [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].
Then read the guidance (AC, AIM) for how to comply, remembering it does not override the rule [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].
Answer with the citation and show the learner the paragraph.

body.p: Worked example. Question: "After my checkride, can my two friends and I split the rental three ways?" Part 61, private pilot privileges, is 61.113. Paragraph (a) bars acting as PIC for compensation or hire except as listed; paragraph (c) says a private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of the operating expenses, and those expenses may involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]]. A three-way equal split of the rental is the pro rata share.

callout.text: Use guided discussion: open with a lead-off question, steer with follow-up questions, and ask open-ended "what if" questions instead of yes or no ones [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
When the rule text does not settle it, do not guess. The PHAK says questions about pilot certification should go to the local FSDO [[1:24|PHAK 1-9]].

check.q: Your learner reads only the first sentence of 61.113(a) and decides a private pilot can never be paid for anything. What reading habit fixes this?
check.a: Read the whole section: (a) itself says "except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h)", which lists the exceptions [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]].

chunks.title: K2: 49 CFR 830, definitions and immediate notification

body.p: Part 830 is an NTSB rule in Title 49, not an FAA rule. It covers the first notification and later reporting of accidents, incidents and certain other occurrences involving U.S. civil aircraft wherever they happen, and preserving wreckage, mail, cargo and records [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]].

head: Term
What 830.2 says
rows: Aircraft accident
Between the time anyone boards with the intent of flight and all have disembarked, someone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft gets substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Fatal injury
Results in death within 30 days of the accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Serious injury

Hospitalization over 48 hours starting within 7 days of the injury; a fracture of any bone except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose; severe bleeding or nerve, muscle or tendon damage; any internal organ; second or third degree burns, or burns over more than 5 percent of the body [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Substantial damage

Hurts structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement. Not substantial: an engine failure or damage limited to one engine, bent fairings or cowling, dented skin, small punctures, ground damage to propeller blades, and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
Incident
An occurrence other than an accident that affects or could affect the safety of operations [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Operator
Anyone who causes or authorizes the operation, such as the owner, lessee or bailee [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].

body.p: 830.5: the operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, by the most expeditious means available, after an accident, after any listed serious incident, or when an aircraft is overdue and believed to be in an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. The listed incidents that fit a single-engine trainer:

bullets: Flight control system malfunction or failure [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].
A required flight crewmember unable to do normal duties because of injury or illness [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].
In-flight fire, or aircraft collision in flight [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].
Damage to property other than the aircraft estimated over $25,000 to repair (materials and labor), or fair market value if a total loss, whichever is less [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].
Release of all or part of a propeller blade, except when caused solely by ground contact [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].
Complete loss of information, not flickering, from more than 50 percent of the cockpit displays such as EFIS or PFD displays [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].
An ACAS resolution advisory on an IFR flight plan when following it was needed to avoid a substantial risk of collision [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].
The other items cover large multiengine aircraft, turbine engines, helicopter rotors and air carriers [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

callout.text: The NTSB Response Operations Center numbers in the rule are 844-373-9922 or 202-314-6290 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Put them on the school's emergency card.

check.q: A passenger sprains an ankle in a hard landing and stays in the hospital 30 hours. The airplane has only a flat tire. Is this an accident?
check.a: No. A 30-hour stay is not over 48 hours and a sprain is not a listed serious injury, and tire damage is not substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

chunks.title: K2: After the call: preservation, reports and other reporting systems

body.p: When you notify, give what is available: type, nationality and registration; owner and operator; PIC; date and time; last departure point and intended landing point; position from an easily defined point; persons aboard, killed and seriously injured; nature of the event, weather and damage; and any explosives, radioactive or other dangerous articles [[60:883|49 CFR 830.6]] [[60:884|49 CFR 830.6]].

bullets: Preserve wreckage, cargo, mail and all records until the NTSB takes custody or releases them [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
Before the NTSB takes custody, move wreckage only to remove injured or trapped persons, protect the wreckage from further damage, or protect the public from injury [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
If you must move it, make sketches, notes and photographs of the original positions and impact marks if possible [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
Keep all records, reports and memos about the event until the NTSB says otherwise [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
File NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days after an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing. For a listed incident, file only if the NTSB asks [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

Each crewmember who is able attaches a statement; an incapacitated crewmember submits one as soon as able [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]]. File with the NTSB field office nearest the event [[60:885|49 CFR 830.15(c)]].

head: Other report
What it is
Key points
rows: NASA ASRS
Voluntary FAA program, with NASA as the independent third party [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]].

Waives certain disciplinary action for timely reports, delivered or postmarked within 10 days [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]]. The FAA will not use the reports in enforcement, except information on accidents or criminal offenses [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]].
Near midair collision
Possible collision from proximity under 500 feet, or a reported collision hazard [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].
Say "I wish to report a near midair collision" to ATC or FSS by radio or phone [[34:178|AIM 7-7-3]].
91.3(c) deviation report
Written report after an emergency deviation [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].
Sent only on request of the Administrator [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

callout.text: AIM 7-7-2 repeats the NTSB list, but it is shorter than current 830.5 and lacks the propeller blade, display and ACAS items [[34:176|AIM 7-7-2]] [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. Teach from 49 CFR 830.

check.q: A crewmember was hospitalized and could not sign a statement when the accident report was filed. What does 830.15 require?
check.a: An incapacitated crewmember submits the statement as soon as physically able [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

chunks.title: K3: Advisory Circulars, InFOs and SAFOs

body.p: An AC is an informational document the FAA wants to distribute, from a one-page notice to a textbook-length guide. ACs are for information only and are not regulations, and all current and historical ACs are on the FAA website [[1:25|PHAK 1-10]]. The AIM adds that ACs are issued in a numbered subject system matching the CFR, and are not binding unless incorporated into a regulation by reference [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].

bullets: Why an AC exists: to give an acceptable, clearly understood method to comply with a regulation, standardize how a rule is applied, clear up a common misunderstanding, help industry implement a rule, or expand on safety standards [[1:25|PHAK 1-10]] [[1:26|PHAK 1-11]].

Reading the number: the first part is the subject area matching a 14 CFR part, the part after the dash is the sequence, and the letter shows the revision; a first version has no letter [[1:26|PHAK 1-11]].
The library's AC on pilot and instructor certification is AC 61-65K [[12:1|AC 61-65K]].

head: AC a CFI uses
Why
rows: Sample endorsements and part 61 guidance (taught in AI.II.K) [[12:1|AC 61-65K]]
Pilot's Guide to a Preflight Briefing, which the AIM tells pilots to review [[33:323|AIM 5-1-2]]
Describes the Aviation Safety Reporting Program [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]]
Aeronautical decision making [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]
English language skill standards, for learners who struggle with English [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]
FAA-approved flight instructor refresher courses [[25:168|AIH 8-10]]

bullets: SAFO: important, often time-critical safety information that may recommend non-regulatory action; the audience can include general aviation operators [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].
InFO: similar, but lower urgency, helping operators meet administrative or certain regulatory requirements [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].
Both are on the FAA website with a free email subscription [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].

check.q: In "AC 61-65K", what does the 61 tell you?
check.a: The subject area, which matches 14 CFR part 61 [[1:26|PHAK 1-11]].

body.p: Under 61.43(a), a practical test consists of performing the tasks in the areas of operation of the applicable ACS or PTS, incorporated by reference and listed in appendix A to part 61; demonstrating mastery of the aircraft; performing within the approved standards; and showing sound judgment [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]] [[60:223|14 CFR 61.43(a)]] [[60:199|14 CFR 61.14]].

bullets: Private pilot, airplane: FAA-S-ACS-6C, November 2023 [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]].
Commercial pilot, airplane: FAA-S-ACS-7B, November 2023 [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]].
Instrument rating, airplane: FAA-S-ACS-8C; flight instructor, airplane: FAA-S-ACS-25, November 2023 [[60:383|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]].

body.p: The ACS and PTS are testing documents, not teaching documents, and not a syllabus. The instructor trains the applicant to acceptable standards in everything the tasks cover, and the latest version with all changes should be used for training [[24:30|AFH 1-9]]. The AIH adds that certification standards cover only the most critical job tasks, so tests do not represent an entire syllabus, and instructors should not limit their objectives to the minimum requirements [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

bullets: Use the ACS to set performance objectives for each lesson [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].
Teach the maneuvers the ACS lists, but present the objectives in scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].
Mark progress against it: tell the learner when performance nears, meets and exceeds the ACS [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].
Each Task in this CFI ACS lists Knowledge (K), Risk management (R) and Skills (S) elements, such as AI.II.J.K1 to AI.II.J.S1 (ACS AI.II.J).

check.q: Which part 61 section makes the ACS the standard for a practical test?
check.a: 61.43(a)(1), which points to the ACS/PTS incorporated by reference in 61.14 and listed in appendix A [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]] [[60:199|14 CFR 61.14]].

head: Document
Approved?
What it is
rows: Owner or information manual
Not FAA approved
General information on the make and model, not for one airplane, not kept current, and never a substitute for the AFM/POH [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
Airplane Flight Manual (AFM)
FAA approved
Procedures and limitations for that make and model, usually by serial number; part 91 requires compliance with its limitations, markings and placards [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH)
Contains FAA-approved AFM information
The title page must say which sections are FAA approved as the AFM; for most light airplanes built after 1975 the POH is also the approved flight manual [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

body.p: 91.9 makes it a rule: no one may operate without complying with the AFM limitations, markings and placards, and a current, approved AFM (or, where none is required, approved manual material, markings and placards) must be available in a U.S.-registered aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]. The serial number and registration go on the title page; a manual without them is for general study only [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

head: GAMA section
What to teach from it
rows: 1 General
Dimensions and the definitions and abbreviations used in the book [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
2 Limitations
Airspeed, powerplant, weight and loading, flight limits and placards [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]] [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
3 Emergency Procedures
Memorize immediate action items, then use the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
4 Normal Procedures
Checklists plus amplified procedures [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
5 Performance
Takeoff, climb, cruise, landing and stall data [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
6 Weight and Balance/Equipment List
All the data needed to compute weight and balance [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
7 Systems Description
How the systems work [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]
8 Handling, Service and Maintenance
Inspections and preventive maintenance a pilot may do [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]]
9 Supplements
Optional equipment such as autopilots and navigation systems, inserted when installed [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]]

check.q: Your learner wants the limitations for the airplane's added GPS navigator. Which POH section?
check.a: Section 9, Supplements, which covers optional equipment and is added when the equipment is installed [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].

chunks.title: K6: The AIM and its companion publications

body.p: The AIM gives basic flight information and ATC procedures for the U.S. NAS. It also covers health and medical facts, flight safety factors, a Pilot/Controller Glossary, and safety, accident and hazard reporting; the international version is the AIP [[33:52|AIM Basic Flight Information]]. The PHAK calls it the official guide to basic flight information and ATC procedures [[1:24|PHAK 1-9]].

Its own policy statement says the AIM is not regulatory. It shows techniques and procedures that may be required by other publications or regulations, and it exists to help pilots meet those responsibilities [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]].

bullets: Numbering: chapter, section, paragraph. Paragraph 1-1-1 is chapter 1 (Air Navigation), section 1 (Navigation Aids), paragraph 1 [[33:55|AIM Table of Contents]].
Schedule: a Basic manual and three changes. Basic 2/20/25, Change 1 8/7/25, Change 2 1/22/26, Change 3 7/9/26, then a new Basic on 12/24/26 [[33:52|AIM Publication Schedule]].
Each change opens with an Explanation of Changes listing what moved [[33:3|AIM Explanation of Changes]].
Users are responsible for viewing, downloading and subscribing to change notices [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]].
Companion: the Chart Supplement, with airports, communications, NAVAIDs, VOR checkpoints and special notices [[33:52|AIM Basic Flight Information]], issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]].

head: AIM paragraph
Use it to teach
rows: Good preflight habits even under VFR: full briefing, NOTAMs, flight plan, current charts [[33:323|AIM 5-1-2]] [[33:324|AIM 5-1-2]]
ASRS, accident and incident reporting, near midair collisions, SAFOs and InFOs [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]] [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]]
FAA Safety Alerts, Charting Notices and Data Product Notices about chart products [[34:190|AIM 9-1-3]]
What each chart series is and how often it is revised [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]]

check.q: What does AIM paragraph number 7-7-5 tell you before you even read it?
check.a: Chapter 7, section 7, paragraph 5, which is the SAFO and InFO paragraph [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].

chunks.title: R1: Expired charts, manuals and publications

body.p: Aeronautical information changes fast. The Chart Users' Guide says to check the effective date on every chart and publication, use current editions and discard obsolete ones. The next scheduled edition date is printed on the cover, 0901Z is the changeover time, and NOTAMs carry changes between cycles [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]]. Sectional and terminal area charts are revised every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide, VFR Symbology]].

head: Out of date item
Hazard
What to teach
rows: Chart
Changed airspace, frequencies or obstacles; the guide says current editions avoid danger [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]].
Read the cover dates on preflight, check NOTAMs, and "use current charts" [[33:324|AIM 5-1-2]].
Navigation database
Named waypoints may no longer exist or may have moved [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
Check currency and update; if you cannot, ignore the moving map airspace for critical decisions and verify waypoints on a current chart [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
POH/AFM
Wrong limitations or missing supplements; an owner's manual is not kept current [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
91.9 requires a current, approved AFM in the aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]].
ACS or PTS
Training to the wrong standard.
Use the edition listed in appendix A to part 61 [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]], with all recent changes [[24:30|AFH 1-9]].
Handbooks and AIM
Old procedures. The PHAK itself warns that its references may not all be current [[1:5|PHAK v]].
Read the AIM Explanation of Changes and subscribe to notices [[33:3|AIM Explanation of Changes]] [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]].

body.p: 91.103 requires the PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. Use it with the learner to frame the question: is an old chart really all the information available?

callout.text: Your own library is part of this risk. Learners copy what you carry. FI.I.E covers why the AIH wants instructors to keep current publications.

check.q: Where on a printed VFR chart do you confirm it is still current?
check.a: The next scheduled edition date printed on the cover [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]].

chunks.title: S1: Teaching publications, and how the examiner checks it

body.p: The examiner will ask you to teach at least one of K1 through K6 (ACS AI.II.J.S1). Choose one you can teach well from the source itself, for example 49 CFR 830 or answering a part 61 question, and bring the current text.

Finding and reading a regulation is a mental skill that needs practice, so the demonstration-performance method fits. It has five phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance, instructor supervision and evaluation [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

bullets: Explanation: show the map of publications and how 14 CFR is built (chunks 1 and 2); state the end result you want [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
Demonstration: think aloud while you find 61.57(b) and read it to the last subparagraph; leave out anything extra [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].
Performance and supervision: the learner finds the 91.409(b) answer for a rental airplane while you coach [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].
Evaluation: the learner answers a new question alone and cites the paragraph; you judge it [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

body.p: For 49 CFR 830, use short real-world problems. The AIH says good problems relate to the real world, require decisions and connect old and new knowledge [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. A one-page case (bent prop, cracked spar, broken aileron cable) works better than reading the definitions aloud.

callout.text: Teach with the learner's own device and an electronic copy of the current rules. The AIH notes that most FAA regulations, standards and guides are available electronically [[25:169|AIH 8-11]].

check.q: In demonstration-performance, which two phases happen at the same time?

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Treating the AIM or an AC as a rule, or as "just advice" to ignore
"The AIM says I must..." or "It's only an AC."

Show the AIM policy statement and the AC rule: guidance, but often the way to meet a rule [[33:53|AIM Flight Information Publication Policy]] [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].
Reading only the first sentence
A wrong yes or no on 61.113 or 61.57
Read to the end of the section, including "except as provided" [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].
One "night"
A learner flies passengers at dusk or skips position lights
Teach the three periods side by side [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].
Using AIM 7-7-2 as the NTSB list
Misses propeller blade, display and ACAS events
Calling every scrape an accident, or no event an accident
Confusion after a prop strike or a wingtip hit
Check 830.2: injuries and substantial damage, with its exclusions [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
Wrong manual in the airplane
An owner's manual, or a POH for another serial number
91.9 requires a current, approved AFM; the title page must show this airplane [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]] [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].
Expired chart or database
Cover date passed; database warning on the GPS
Current edition, NOTAMs, update or verify on a current chart [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]] [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
Guessing
A confident answer with no citation
Admit it, and look it up with the learner [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

check.q: A learner insists a bent propeller tip from a runway strike, with nothing else damaged and no one hurt, must be reported to the NTSB at once. What do you show her?
check.a: 830.2: ground damage to propeller blades is not substantial damage, and 830.5(a)(8) excludes blade release caused solely by ground contact [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

scenario.title: Maya's list of questions
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Maya, a private pilot learner about three weeks from her checkride, arrives for a Saturday ground lesson with a page of questions she collected during the week. You have the current 14 CFR, 49 CFR 830, the AIM and the club airplane's POH open on the table.

questions.q: "After my checkride, can two friends and I split the club airplane's rental three ways for a beach trip?" How do you answer, and how do you teach it?
questions.a: Open 61.113 with her. Paragraph (a) bars a private pilot from acting as PIC for compensation or hire except as listed; paragraph (c) allows sharing as long as she pays at least the pro rata share of fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees [[60:307|14 CFR 61.113(a)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]]. An equal three-way split is her pro rata share.

questions.q: "Where do I even start looking?" What do you show her first?
questions.a: The map: part 61 covers certification, knowledge, proficiency, training and testing, and part 91 covers general, VFR and IFR flight rules [[1:23|PHAK 1-8]]. Then the subpart titles, for example private pilots in part 61 subpart E [[60:176|14 CFR Part 61 contents]].

questions.q: "My paper sectional at home expired last month, but it's fine for a local flight, right?"
questions.a: No. The Chart Users' Guide says to use current editions, discard obsolete ones, check the next edition date on the cover and check NOTAMs between cycles [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]]; sectionals are revised every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]].

questions.q: "If I scrape a wingtip on a hangar while taxiing out, do I have to call the NTSB?"
questions.a: Wingtip damage is listed as not substantial damage, so with no death or serious injury it is not an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]]. It becomes reportable only if something on the 830.5 list happens, such as property damage over $25,000 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

questions.q: "Which ACS will my examiner use? I downloaded one from a forum dated June 2018."
questions.a: The one listed in appendix A to part 61 for her certificate: FAA-S-ACS-6C, November 2023 [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]], which 61.43 makes the test standard [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]]. Have her download it from the FAA, not a forum.

questions.q: Maya reads 61.57(a)(1) and says she cannot fly solo unless she has done 3 landings in 90 days. Is she right, and what reading error is this?
questions.a: No. 61.57(a)(1) applies to acting as PIC of an aircraft carrying persons, and (a)(2) lets a pilot regain it as PIC under day VFR with no one else aboard [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]]. She stopped before reading the whole section.

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Teach at least one of the elements listed in K1 through K6" (ACS AI.II.J.S1). Expect to pick a topic, for example 49 CFR 830 or a part 61/91 legal question, and teach it from the current source: state the objective, show where the rule lives, read it accurately to the end, and check the examiner-learner's understanding with an open question.
skills.practice: Build three 10-minute lessons: the CFR map and "Is this legal?" method, 49 CFR 830 with three short cases, and the POH sections. Teach each one to a fellow applicant using demonstration-performance [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:125|AIH 5-22]], and have them hand you a question you did not prepare so you practice looking it up out loud [[25:143|AIH 6-12]].

quiz.q: Which publication's contents bind the public only if a regulation incorporates them by reference?
options: 14 CFR part 91
An Advisory Circular
49 CFR part 830
The AFM limitations section
quiz.why: The AIM says AC contents are not binding unless incorporated into a regulation by reference [[33:54|AIM Code of Federal Regulations and Advisory Circulars]].

options: The title
The part
The section
The paragraph
quiz.why: Part 61, Certification: Pilots, Flight Instructors, and Ground Instructors; 61.57 is the section within it [[60:174|14 CFR Part 61]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].

options: Only the items listed
Includes but is not limited to
Includes, at the Administrator's option
Includes, unless a part says otherwise
quiz.why: Includes means includes but is not limited to [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].

quiz.q: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, what does 91.3 allow?
options: Any pilot aboard may deviate from any rule
The PIC may deviate from part 91 to the extent required, and report in writing if asked
The PIC may deviate only with ATC approval
The PIC must report every deviation within 10 days
quiz.why: The PIC may deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent required, and must send a written report on request of the Administrator [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

quiz.q: Under 61.113(c), which expenses may a private pilot share with passengers?
options: Fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees
Any cost, if the passengers are friends
Fuel only
Fuel, maintenance and insurance
quiz.why: The pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share, and the expenses may involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(c)]].

quiz.q: Which of these is substantial damage under 49 CFR 830.2?
options: Dented skin
Damage to the brakes
Damage that hurts structural strength and would normally need major repair
Damage limited to one engine
quiz.why: Substantial damage adversely affects structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair; the other three are listed exclusions [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

quiz.q: In AC 61-65K, what does the letter K show?
options: The subject area
The sequence number in the subject area
The revision of the AC
The office that wrote it
quiz.why: The letter shows the revision sequence; a first version has no letter [[1:26|PHAK 1-11]].

quiz.q: A manual in the airplane has no registration or serial number on its title page. What is it good for?
options: It satisfies 91.9 if it is the right model
General study purposes only
Emergency procedures only
Weight and balance only
quiz.why: A manual that does not show a specific aircraft's registration and serial number is limited to general study purposes [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

quiz.q: Where do you see what changed in the newest AIM change?
options: Chapter 1, section 1
The Explanation of Changes at the front
The Pilot/Controller Glossary
The index
quiz.why: Each AIM change begins with an Explanation of Changes listing the changed paragraphs [[33:3|AIM Explanation of Changes]].

quiz.q: What time of day does the Chart Users' Guide give as the changeover time for new FAA charts and publications?
options: 1200 local
0000 local
quiz.why: 0901Z is the changeover time for updated aeronautical information and products in the United States [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide 6]].

final_quiz.q: Sunset is 1730. Your learner, a private pilot with three day landings last week but no night landings in a year, plans a pattern flight with a passenger from 1735 to a full stop at 1820. Which statement is correct?
options: Illegal: it is after sunset, so 61.57(b) applies
Legal under 61.57, but position lights must be on because it is after sunset
Illegal: 1.1 night starts at sunset
Legal, and no lights are needed until civil twilight ends
final_quiz.why: The 61.57(b) period starts 1 hour after sunset (1830), so day currency covers this flight [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]], but 91.209 requires lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

final_quiz.q: A student taxiing out for a solo flight hits a fuel truck. Nobody is hurt, but a wing spar is cracked and must be replaced. What does 49 CFR 830 require?
options: Nothing; ground events are never accidents
An accident: notify the nearest NTSB office immediately
An incident: file Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days
Only an FAA report
final_quiz.why: The student boarded with intent of flight and the airplane received substantial damage, so it is an accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], requiring immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

final_quiz.q: After a hard landing a passenger has a simple fracture of a finger. The airplane has only a damaged tire and a bent wheel fairing. Is it an accident?
options: Yes, any fracture is a serious injury
No, a simple finger fracture is excluded and the damage is not substantial
Yes, because a passenger was hurt
Only if the passenger is hospitalized
final_quiz.why: Simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose are excluded from serious injury, and tire and fairing damage are not substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner plans a flight 8 NM off the coast. She asks whether part 91 applies out there. The best answer is:
options: No, part 91 ends at the shoreline
Between 3 and 12 NM offshore she must comply with the part 91 sections listed in 91.1(b)
All of part 91 applies to any distance
Only the VFR weather rules apply
final_quiz.why: Part 91 governs operations within the U.S. including waters within 3 NM; between 3 and 12 NM a listed set of sections applies [[60:435|14 CFR 91.1]].

final_quiz.q: A learner brings his own airplane and pays you for instruction. Its annual is current, but it has flown 120 hours since its last 100-hour inspection. Does 91.409(b) stop you from instructing?
options: Yes, any instruction for hire needs a 100-hour
No, because you did not provide the aircraft
Yes, unless you hold an A&P
No, but only for dual on local flights
final_quiz.why: 91.409(b) applies to giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]].

final_quiz.q: The club's C172 carries a POH whose title page shows another airplane's serial number and registration. Your learner says it is the same model, so it is fine. Your answer:
options: Fine, POHs are model-specific
Not acceptable: 91.9 requires a current, approved AFM for this airplane, and a manual without this airplane's identity is for general study only
Fine if it has the same revision date
Fine for VFR only
final_quiz.why: 91.9(b) requires a current, approved AFM available in the aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]], and each AFM/POH is unique to its airplane by serial number and registration [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

final_quiz.q: During a cross-country your learner's panel GPS warns that its database expired three weeks ago and no update is possible. What does the PHAK say to do?
options: Keep using it normally for VFR
Disregard the moving map airspace for critical decisions and verify waypoints on a current chart
Divert immediately; flight with an expired database is illegal
Use it only for altitude
final_quiz.why: If an expired database cannot be updated, disregard moving map airspace for critical navigation decisions; waypoints may be gone or moved, so verify them against a current chart [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

final_quiz.q: A school's procedures manual quotes a SAFO's recommended action and says "Required by FAA regulation." What is accurate?
options: Correct; SAFOs are rules
Incorrect; a SAFO may contain recommended, non-regulatory action
Correct only for part 91 operators
Incorrect; SAFOs apply only to airlines
final_quiz.why: SAFOs may contain recommended (non-regulatory) action, and their audience can include general aviation operators [[34:179|AIM 7-7-5]].

final_quiz.q: After an accident, a fuel fire is spreading toward the wreckage before the NTSB arrives. May the wreckage be moved?
options: No, never before NTSB custody
Yes, to protect it from further damage, documenting its positions first if possible
Yes, but only by the FAA
Only to clear the runway for traffic
final_quiz.why: Wreckage may be moved to protect it from further damage, and sketches, notes and photographs should be made of the original positions if possible [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

final_quiz.q: Your commercial applicant has been studying the June 2018 ACS shown in an AIH figure. What should you do?
options: Nothing; the AIH is current
Switch to the edition listed in appendix A to part 61, FAA-S-ACS-7B, November 2023
Use the PTS instead
Use whichever edition the examiner prefers
final_quiz.why: Appendix A lists FAA-S-ACS-7B for the commercial airplane certificate [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]], and 61.43 makes the listed ACS the test standard [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A club member is three hours overdue and believed to have crashed. What does part 830 require?
options: Nothing until the wreckage is found
The operator notifies the NTSB immediately, and files a report if the aircraft is still missing after 7 days
The FSDO handles all overdue aircraft
A report within 10 days only
final_quiz.why: An overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident requires immediate notification [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]], and a report is filed after 7 days if it is still missing [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner cannot find "complex airplane" in 14 CFR 1.1. Where is it defined?
options: The AIM glossary only
It is not defined
final_quiz.why: 61.1(b) defines complex airplane for part 61 [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1(b)]].

final_quiz.q: A student pilot arrives for a solo with her student pilot certificate but left her driver's license and all other photo ID at home. What does 61.3(a) say?
options: She may fly; photo ID is only for checkrides
She may not serve as a required pilot without a photo ID in her possession or readily accessible
She may fly in the pattern only
Her logbook can stand in for ID
final_quiz.why: 61.3(a)(2) requires a photo identification in the person's physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]].

takeaways: 14 CFR and 49 CFR 830 bind; the AIM, ACs, SAFOs and InFOs guide. AFM limitations bind through 91.9, and the ACS through 61.43.
Read a rule to the end: definitions first, then every "except as provided".
Three nights: civil twilight (1.1), 1 hour after sunset (61.57(b)), sunset (91.209).
NTSB: immediate notice for accidents, listed incidents and overdue aircraft; report within 10 days after an accident; incidents only on request.
Know the 830.2 exclusions: prop ground damage, gear, tires, flaps, brakes and wingtips are not substantial damage.
Use current charts, databases, manuals, ACS and AIM, and teach learners to check dates every time.
When you do not know, say so and look it up with the learner.
cfi_notes: AIM 7-7-2 lists the NTSB incidents with older turbine wording and leaves out several current 830.5 items (propeller blade release, loss of more than 50 percent of displays, ACAS resolution advisories, rotor damage and air carrier runway events) [[34:176|AIM 7-7-2]] [[34:177|AIM 7-7-2]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]]. Teach 49 CFR 830.5.

AIH Figure 5-5 shows June 2018 ACS covers [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]; appendix A to part 61 now lists FAA-S-ACS-6C, 7B, 8C and 25, all November 2023 [[60:381|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]] [[60:383|14 CFR part 61 appendix A]]. Teach from appendix A.
PHAK 1-11 uses AC 61-65E as its numbering example [[1:26|PHAK 1-11]]; the library's current edition is AC 61-65K [[12:1|AC 61-65K]]. Use the example to teach the numbering, not the edition.

PHAK 1-10 describes the AIM as sold by subscription through the GPO bookstore [[1:25|PHAK 1-10]]; the AIM itself now says it is posted on the FAA website, distributed electronically, and that users are responsible for subscribing to change notices [[33:50|AIM Subscription Information]]. Teach the AIM's own statement.

AFH 1-9 calls the ACS and PTS testing documents, not teaching documents [[24:30|AFH 1-9]]. That still holds, but current 61.43(a)(1) also makes the ACS/PTS the binding test standard through incorporation by reference [[60:222|14 CFR 61.43(a)]] [[60:199|14 CFR 61.14]]. Teach both halves.
The "three nights" are the most common source of wrong answers. Have learners build a one-line table with 1.1, 61.57(b) and 91.209 in their own words.
Before teaching any rule, ask the learner to find and read its applicability and definitions sections aloud (91.1, 61.1). It trains the "read to the end" habit that most errors come from missing.
Part 830 defines substantial damage but does not say who estimates it. Application: when a mechanic's estimate is not yet available and the damage might be substantial, calling the NTSB costs little.

ASRS and NTSB reports are separate: the ASRS is a voluntary FAA program run by NASA [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]], while 830.5 notification is a duty of the operator [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Filing one never satisfies the other.
gaps: AC 00-2 (the AC checklist) and the FAA Chief Counsel's legal interpretations are not in this library. For close calls such as cost sharing beyond the rule text, read the interpretations or ask the FSDO.
No source here names a part 91 rule that requires a current chart by date. The currency guidance comes from the Chart Users' Guide, the AIM and 91.103's "all available information".
49 CFR 830 does not say who decides whether damage is substantial, or how to estimate it before a mechanic inspects the airplane.
The ACS's own introduction (element coding, how examiners pick elements) is not in the library; read it in the current FAA-S-ACS-25.
Specific limitations, supplements and revision status come only from the actual airplane's POH/AFM and its revision log.
The NTSB's own online reporting steps are not described in these sources beyond the phone numbers and Form 6120.1/2 in part 830.

activities.title: Where each part lives
activities.intro: Drag each part to the subchapter row that holds it.

activities.title: True or false: reading 14 CFR
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In 14 CFR, "shall" is used in an imperative sense.
"No person may" means a person is permitted but not required.
cards.why: False. It means no person is required, authorized or permitted to do the act [[60:22|14 CFR 1.3]].

cards.s: Night under 14 CFR 1.1 begins at sunset.
cards.why: False. It begins at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

cards.s: 61.57(b) night currency counts takeoffs and landings to a full stop made from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
Lighted position lights are required from sunset to sunrise.
Part 61 has no definitions of its own; all of them are in part 1.
cards.why: False. 61.1(b) defines terms such as complex airplane and cross-country time [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1(b)]].

cards.s: A word written in the singular in 14 CFR also covers the plural.

activities.title: Count the days, dollars and hours
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: An accident happens on November 3. What is the latest day of November to file NTSB Form 6120.1/2?
items.why: Within 10 days after the accident: November 3 + 10 days = November 13 [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

items.q: A student's runway excursion destroys a fence. The repair estimate is $11,250 in materials and $14,900 in labor. By how many dollars does it exceed the 830.5 property damage threshold?
Sunset is 1752 local. From what local time (hhmm) do landings count toward 61.57(b) passenger night currency?
Your learner's printed AIM is the Basic of 2/20/25 with no changes inserted. How many changes has she missed as of October 2026?
items.why: Change 1 (8/7/25), Change 2 (1/22/26) and Change 3 (7/9/26) are all effective by October 2026: 3 changes [[33:52|AIM Publication Schedule]].

items.q: You provide the airplane for paid instruction. Its 100-hour was due at 2,440.0 hours; you flew it to the shop and the inspection was done at 2,446.0. At what time in service is the next 100-hour due?
items.why: The 6 excess ferry hours count toward the next 100: 2,446.0 + 100 - 6.0 = 2,540.0, the same as 2,440.0 + 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

activities.title: Chief instructor on a bad day
activities.intro: You are the chief instructor at a small school. It is Saturday, and the phone keeps ringing.

steps.s: 0900: a renter calls. On landing the propeller tips struck the runway and curled. Nobody is hurt and a walkaround shows no other damage. Do you call the NTSB now?
options: Yes, any propeller damage is an accident
No, ground damage to propeller blades is not substantial damage and no one is hurt
Only after a mechanic quotes a new propeller
File Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days instead
steps.why: Ground damage to propeller blades is not substantial damage, and blade release caused solely by ground contact is excluded from 830.5 [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]].

steps.s: 1100: a solo student radios that her right aileron cable has failed. She lands safely with no damage. What now?
options: Nothing, there was no damage
Notify the nearest NTSB office immediately: flight control system failure
File an ASRS report only
Call the FSDO next week
steps.why: A flight control system malfunction or failure is a listed serious incident requiring immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

steps.s: On the phone, the NTSB asks for information. Which set is required, if available?
options: Only the N-number
Type, nationality and registration; owner and operator; PIC; date and time; departure and destination; position; persons aboard and injured; nature, weather and damage; dangerous articles
The student's logbook totals and medical class
The maintenance logs only

steps.s: Must the school file Form 6120.1/2 for the aileron event within 10 days?
options: Yes, every notification needs one
Only if an NTSB representative asks for it
Only if the airplane is damaged later
Yes, within 7 days
steps.why: A report on an incident that required immediate notification is filed only as requested by an authorized NTSB representative [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

steps.s: The student asks if a NASA ASRS report would replace the NTSB call.
options: Yes, it covers everything
No. ASRS is a separate voluntary FAA program run by NASA; the operator's 830.5 duty stands
Yes, if filed within 10 days
No, students cannot file ASRS reports
steps.why: ASRS is a voluntary program with NASA as a third party [[34:176|AIM 7-7-1]], and the FAA will not use those reports in enforcement except for accidents or criminal offenses [[60:440|14 CFR 91.25]]; the 830.5 notification is a separate duty [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].
